title: Weaker write path, stronger retention: series-stacked gain-cell write transistors
idea: Paradox: a slower write device yields a stronger hold. In a capacitorless 2T gain cell (storage node = read-FET gate) the write device is split into two series transistors on separate gates, both pulsed on to write; in hold the middle node self-biases the upper device to negative VGS (stack effect), and a leakage-tail outlier now needs both devices defective at once.
why: Tail probability p becomes ~p^2 (e.g. 1e-5 to 1e-10 of cells below spec) plus ~10x nominal leakage cut, removing retention profiling and stretching refresh 10-100x with no capacitor.

title: Too off to use electrically: light-gated photoconductor gain-cell write path
idea: Paradox: a switch useless electrically is ideal optically. The gain cell's write transistor is replaced by a gateless a-Si:H photoconductor bridge from write bitline to read-FET gate, addressed by an on-chip waveguide/micro-LED row bus; dark conductivity ~1e-11 S/cm gives ~1e-17 A hold leakage with no gate field and hence no GIDL, while illumination raises conduction 1e5-1e6x for writing.
why: Second-to-minute retention with no storage capacitor, no wordline pump (fact 10) and no GIDL tail (fact 3); low-temperature BEOL/panel compatible; main risk is reaching ~10 ns photoconductive write.

title: Every bit everywhere: Walsh-spread storage across multilevel capacitorless cells
idea: Paradox: each bit lives everywhere and nowhere. A block of N bits is written as the N analog levels of its Walsh-Hadamard transform into multilevel FeFET or gain cells; reading applies the inverse transform and slices, so a dead, stuck or drifted cell becomes small noise spread over all N bits instead of a hard error on one.
why: With N=64 a fully failed cell perturbs each bit by ~1/8 swing, absorbed without ECC, so capacitorless cells with ~1e-3 defect density become usable (cost per bit, yield).

title: Flash that forgets lasts forever: shallow-trap volatile charge cells
idea: Paradox: giving up permanence buys unlimited endurance. A 1T charge-trap transistor uses a thin engineered trap layer and 1.5-2 nm tunnel oxide sized for ~1 s retention, programmed by direct tunneling at ~2-3 V in 10-50 ns; with no Fowler-Nordheim high-field stress, the oxide wear that limits flash endurance practically vanishes, and the cell is refreshed about once a second.
why: Capacitorless ~4F^2 1T cell with refresh ~15x rarer than DRAM's 64 ms and >1e15 endurance target, built in any NOR/logic fab (U.S.-manufacturable).

title: Static memory run dynamically: duty-cycled SRAM supply regeneration
idea: Paradox: a static cell is operated as a dynamic one to kill its leakage. Large SRAM arrays power-gate their cell supply most of the time, letting each latch hold its state on parasitic node charge for ~0.1-1 us, then pulse VDD on for a few ns per row group so the cross-coupled pair regenerates to full rail, a refresh needing no storage capacitor or sense amp.
why: ~5-10% supply duty cuts SRAM array leakage ~10x, making large SRAM capacity on mature U.S. logic nodes more viable as a DRAM substitute tier; regeneration timing set from on-die leakage monitors.

title: Soft to write, hard to keep: VCMA-locked MRAM standby
idea: Paradox: one magnet is both easy to flip and hard to disturb, separated in time. Perpendicular MTJs are built with low intrinsic barrier (delta ~30, cheap to write) and a shared gate plate applies voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy in standby to raise the barrier toward delta ~60; the boost is removed only on the row being written.
why: Separates the retention-vs-write-error trade: ~2x lower write current and smaller access transistor with NV-class retention; capacitorless; risk is needed VCMA coefficient (~5-10x today's).

title: Friction makes motion exact: ratchet-notch racetrack with barcode guard domains
idea: Paradox: pinning, racetrack memory's classic failure, becomes its registration. Asymmetric sawtooth notches make each current pulse move domain walls exactly one notch, suppressing over/under-shift, and known 'barcode' domain patterns inserted every 32 bits let the read head detect any residual slip and re-shift.
why: Cuts shift-position errors from ~1e-4 to <1e-12 per operation at ~3% capacity overhead, unlocking capacitorless multi-bit-per-access-transistor tracks.

title: The heat that ruins DRAM keeps it: VO2 hysteresis-window cells
idea: Paradox: temperature, DRAM's retention enemy, becomes the retention mechanism. Doped VO2 nanoislands are held by logic waste heat plus a trim heater inside their insulator-metal hysteresis window (~60-68 C) where both phases are stable; a current pulse heats an island metallic (1), a cooling/field pulse returns it insulating (0), read by a 1e2-1e4 resistance ratio.
why: No charge, no leakage tail: state is a structural phase; capacitorless, sub-ns switching reported, best stacked monolithically over hot logic; risks are hysteresis uniformity and write energy.

title: Volatile data, nonvolatile parity: diverse-physics ECC sidecar
idea: Paradox: deliberately mismatched technologies for data and parity. Data lives in capacitorless IGZO gain-cell arrays while ECC check symbols live in an MRAM sidecar on the logic die; leakage/disturb failures and magnetic thermal-flip/write errors are statistically independent, so correlated row/column/mat failures that defeat same-technology ECC become decodable, and parity survives power loss.
why: Correlated failures dominate DUEs; diversity converts many to correctable, letting gain cells ship with a 10-100x weaker retention-tail spec; MRAM endurance (>1e12) is adequate for parity traffic.

title: Data never stored cannot be corrupted: seed-regenerated tensors
idea: Paradox: absent data is the most reliable data. Pseudo-random-by-construction tensors (random projections, adapter inits, dropout masks, hash/sketch matrices, synthetic-noise buffers) are never written to memory; a counter-based PRNG (Philox) in the accelerator datapath regenerates each tile on demand from a 128-bit seed held in latches.
why: Removes those bytes from capacity and from the error surface (no ECC, no refresh, no capacitor); up to ~5-30% of footprint in some workloads.

title: A crystal defect is the bit: conductive ferroelectric domain-wall memory
idea: Paradox: the defect is the data channel. Bits are the presence/absence of a charged domain wall in a nanoscale LiNbO3 or BiFeO3 mesa between in-plane electrodes; reading senses wall conduction at sub-coercive voltage, so it is non-destructive (no read-then-rewrite fatigue as in FeRAM), and ns field pulses create or erase the wall.
why: Capacitorless nonvolatile cell with ON/OFF >1e3; removing read-induced switching extends effective endurance for read-heavy memory traffic; risks are scaling below 50 nm and write endurance.

title: Forget activations, check them backward: reversible-network dual reconstruction
idea: Paradox: not storing data supplies the redundancy that checks stored data. In reversible networks each layer's input can be read from SRAM or reconstructed exactly from its output; storing a subset of activations and reconstructing the rest gives two independent derivations of overlapping tiles, and mismatching tiles are replaced by the reconstruction.
why: Activation memory down ~2-10x plus ECC-free error detection/correction for SRAM-resident activations on capacitorless accelerators; ~25-30% extra backward compute.

title: Cannot stick because it always dissolves: diffusive-memristor dynamic cells
idea: Paradox: volatility is the reliability mechanism. Ag- or Cu-doped SiOx diffusive memristors form a filament that spontaneously dissolves in ~1-100 ms by interfacial energy and are refreshed by re-forming pulses; ReRAM's dominant hard failure, stuck-on filaments that thicken and cannot reset, cannot develop because every filament must re-nucleate each cycle.
why: Capacitorless 4F^2 stackable crosspoint cells with built-in immunity to stuck-on faults; viable if re-forming energy is ~fJ and endurance reaches 1e9-1e12.

title: Fewer electrons, firmer bits: Coulomb-blockade quantized storage nodes
idea: Paradox: storing almost nothing makes the stored thing indivisible. The gain-cell storage node is a sub-3 nm nanocrystal coupled to a narrow read channel and isolated from the write line by a tunnel junction; Coulomb blockade quantizes the charge so partial leakage is impossible, and escape needs a whole-electron tunneling event suppressed by a charging energy far above kT.
why: Capacitorless sub-4F^2 cell with retention far beyond 64 ms if per-electron read signal (~100 mV) is achieved; risks are dot uniformity and background offset charges.

title: No remanence, yet memory: built-in-bias antiferroelectric FETs
idea: Paradox: a material with no remanent polarization is biased into memory. Antiferroelectric ZrO2 in a FET gate stack, with asymmetric work-function electrodes creating a built-in field that shifts one double-hysteresis loop across zero, gives two states stable at zero bias; switching is a field-induced phase transition with little domain-wall pinning, so fatigue is far lower than ferroelectric HZO.
why: Capacitorless FET memory targeting >1e12 cycles (vs ~1e5-1e10 FeFET) with NV retention, closing the endurance gap that blocked FeFET as DRAM.

title: Protected by topology, not barriers: winding-number nanomagnet ring bits
idea: Paradox: individually unstable magnets form a collectively stable bit. Each bit is the winding number (0 or 1) of magnetization around a ring of 6-8 exchange-coupled low-barrier nanodisks; one disk flipping from thermal noise cannot change the winding number, only a coordinated rotation driven by a spin-orbit current loop through the ring center can.
why: Capacitorless; decouples retention from per-element barrier, potentially ~3x lower write energy than MRAM at equal retention; fabrication speculative.

title: DRAM's nemesis as storage: engineered bistable-defect telegraph cells
idea: Paradox: the defect behind VRT and telegraph noise becomes the bit. One engineered metastable defect (DX-like center whose capture involves lattice relaxation) sits in a nanoscale FET channel; a gate pulse switches its configuration, which modulates channel current >50%, and the configurational barrier, not charge leakage, sets retention.
why: Capacitorless single-transistor cell of minimal size where retention is a tunable activation energy rather than a leakage tail; highly speculative placement and uniformity.

title: The leakage mechanism becomes the lock: TFET write devices
idea: Paradox: band-to-band tunneling, the GIDL mechanism behind DRAM's tail, is made the switch itself. A gain cell's write device is an interband tunnel FET (gated p-i-n); off-state has no thermionic subthreshold path, so hold leakage is set by small ambipolar/generation currents and is nearly temperature-flat, while a write pulse turns tunneling fully on.
why: TFET off-currents ~1e-17-1e-18 A/um reported; temperature-flat retention removes the 2x high-temperature refresh penalty; capacitorless; weak on-current is acceptable for charging a tiny gate node.

title: Three leaky gates, one honest channel: multi-gate majority storage transistor
idea: Paradox: unreliable parts compose a reliable whole inside one device. Each bit is held on three separately written storage gates capacitively coupled to one read channel (neuron-MOS style); the channel conducts only if the coupled sum crosses threshold, so the transistor physically computes majority-of-three in a single sense and any single leaked node is outvoted.
why: Capacitorless; per-bit tail probability p becomes ~3p^2 with ~1.3x area if the three write FETs are stacked in BEOL IGZO tiers, allowing ~10x weaker per-node retention spec with no logic or extra reads.

title: Permanent charge fixes volatile charge: per-cell read-FET threshold trimming
idea: Paradox: a one-time nonvolatile fix makes a volatile cell reliable. At wafer test each capacitorless gain cell's read-transistor threshold is measured and centered by injecting calibrated trapped charge into its high-k gate stack (charge-trap-transistor programming available in standard HKMG logic); the dynamic storage node then operates on a variation-free device.
why: Read-FET Vt sigma ~30-50 mV eats much of gain-cell margin; trimming to <10 mV roughly doubles the usable retention window, ~2-4x less refresh and far fewer weak cells, in logic fabs only.

title: Share failures to win: open failure-commons for capacitorless memory
idea: Paradox: competitors pool their failures to beat a shared rival. A consortium/government-funded open lab runs standardized accelerated retention, disturb and endurance tests on wafers from any capacitorless-memory startup (gain cell, FeFET, AFE, MRAM) and publishes anonymized per-cell failure distributions and physics-of-failure models; participation is a condition of CHIPS-style grants.
why: Tail qualification at 1e-9 and 1000-hour stress costs startups years and ~$10M+; pooled data could halve time-to-qualify and de-risk U.S. alternatives to capacitor DRAM (U.S. manufacturability, capital).
